posts.title: How to Become a Notary Public in Florida
posts.metaTitle: How to Become a Notary Public in Florida (2026 Requirements, Cost & Steps)
posts.metaDesc: Step-by-step requirements to become a Florida notary public in 2026: eligibility, the $7,500 bond, education, application, fees, and how long a commission lasts.
keywords: how to become a notary in florida
posts.excerpt: Florida commissions notaries for four-year terms. Here is exactly what the state requires, what it costs, and how long it takes.

sections.html:
Under Fla. Stat. §117.01(1), an applicant for a Florida notary commission must be at least 18 years old, be a legal resident of the State of Florida, and be able to read, write, and understand the English language.

The statute also requires the application to include the applicant's full name, residence address and telephone number, business address and telephone number, date of birth, and Social Security number. The Social Security number is confidential and exempt from public disclosure under §119.071(5)(a) — it never appears in the public commission record.

An applicant who is not a United States citizen must record a declaration of domicile.

There are three separate costs, and people routinely confuse them.

  • The state filing fee — paid to the Florida Department of State with the application.
  • The $7,500 surety bond — required by §117.01(6). This is not insurance for you. A surety bond pays the public if you make an error, and the surety can then come after you for reimbursement.
  • Errors & omissions insurance — not required by Florida law. E&O is what actually protects the notary. It is optional for a general commission, but it is effectively mandatory if you want signing work, because signing services and title companies set their own minimums.

Most applicants go through a bonding agency, which bundles the bond, the education, the application filing, and a seal into one package. That is why you see quoted prices that bear no relation to the state fee alone.

First-time applicants must complete a state-approved notary education course before applying. Renewing notaries are treated differently from first-time applicants — confirm your current obligation with the Department of State or your bonding agency rather than assuming.

Applications are submitted to the Florida Department of State through a bonding agency. The state issues the commission certificate; the bonding agency typically supplies the seal.

A Florida notary commission runs for four years. Your expiration date appears on your commission and in the public record — you can look up any Florida notary, including yourself, in this register or directly through the Department of State.

Renewal is not automatic. Start roughly 90 days out; a lapse means reapplying rather than renewing, and it takes any Remote Online Notary registration down with it.

Florida caps the fee for the notarial act itself at $10 per act (§117.05) and $25 per online notarization (§117.275). Those caps apply only to the act. Travel, printing, and signing-agent service fees are separate, uncapped, and negotiated directly. That distinction is the entire economics of mobile and loan-signing work — see what a Florida notary can charge.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to become a notary in Florida?
faqs.a: There are three separate costs: the state filing fee paid to the Florida Department of State, the mandatory $7,500 surety bond required by Fla. Stat. 117.01(6), and optional errors and omissions insurance. Most applicants buy a bundled package from a bonding agency that includes the bond, education, filing, and seal.

faqs.q: How long does a Florida notary commission last?
faqs.a: Four years. Renewal is not automatic, and a lapsed commission must be reapplied for rather than renewed. A lapse also terminates any Remote Online Notary registration.

faqs.q: Do I need errors and omissions insurance to be a notary in Florida?
faqs.a: No. Florida law requires a $7,500 surety bond but does not require E&O insurance. However, signing services and title companies set their own E&O minimums, so it is practically necessary for anyone seeking loan signing work.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a notary bond and E&O insurance?
faqs.a: A surety bond protects the public. If you make an error, the bond pays the injured party and the surety can seek reimbursement from you. E&O insurance protects you, covering your own defense and liability for unintentional mistakes.

faqs.q: Can a non-US citizen become a Florida notary?
faqs.a: Yes. A permanent resident who is not a United States citizen may be appointed, but must record a declaration of domicile.

posts.title: How Much Can a Florida Notary Charge?
posts.metaTitle: How Much Can a Florida Notary Charge? Fees, Caps & Travel Costs (2026)
posts.metaDesc: Florida caps notarial acts at $10 and online notarizations at $25. Travel and signing fees are uncapped. Here is what a notary may legally charge and why mobile notaries cost more.
keywords: how much does a notary cost in florida
posts.excerpt: The statutory cap is $10 per act. So why does a mobile notary quote $75? Because the cap covers the act, not the trip.

sections.html:
Florida sets a hard ceiling on the fee for the notarial act itself:

  • $10 per notarial act for traditional, in-person notarization — Fla. Stat. §117.05(2)(a)
  • $25 per notarial act performed by remote online notarization — Fla. Stat. §117.275

An "act" is a single notarization — one acknowledgment, one jurat, one oath. A document requiring three notarizations may be charged three times.

This is where nearly all confusion originates. The caps apply to the notarial act. They do not apply to:

  • Travel — a mobile notary coming to your home, hospital, or office
  • Printing — loan packages routinely run 100–200 pages, often on two paper sizes
  • Signing-agent services — walking a borrower through a closing package, checking completeness, shipping the return
  • After-hours and weekend availability
  • Scanbacks and courier or shipping charges

These are ordinary contract fees negotiated between you and the notary. Florida does not regulate them.

A mobile notary quoting $75 to visit your home for one signature is not overcharging. They are charging $10 for the act and $65 for the trip, and they are entitled to do so — provided the fees are disclosed to you in advance.

A loan signing agent handling a refinance package typically charges $85–$200. That covers printing the package, travelling to the borrower, sitting through a 45–90 minute signing, and shipping the documents back — with only the notarizations themselves subject to the statutory cap.

Ask for the total in advance and get it in writing. A notary should be able to break the quote into the act fee and everything else. A notary may not charge for the act beyond the cap, and may not condition the notarization on buying another service.

Also worth knowing: a notary cannot give you legal advice, choose your document, or explain its legal effect. That is the practice of law. If the notary is telling you what a document means for your situation, something is wrong.

faqs.q: How much can a notary charge in Florida?
faqs.a: Florida caps the notarial act at $10 per act under Fla. Stat. 117.05(2)(a), and at $25 per act for remote online notarization under Fla. Stat. 117.275. Travel, printing, and signing-agent service fees are not capped and are negotiated separately.

faqs.q: Why do mobile notaries charge $75 or more in Florida?
faqs.a: Because the $10 cap applies only to the notarial act. Travel to your location is a separate, uncapped service fee. A $75 quote is typically $10 for the act and $65 for travel and convenience.

faqs.q: How much does a loan signing agent charge in Florida?
faqs.a: Typically $85 to $200 per signing, depending on the loan product. That covers printing a 100 to 200 page package, travel, conducting the signing, and shipping documents back. Only the notarizations themselves are capped at $10 each.

faqs.q: Can a Florida notary charge more than $10 per signature?
faqs.a: Not for the notarial act itself. A notary may charge separately for travel, printing, and other services, but the act is capped at $10, or $25 for an online notarization.

faqs.q: Does a notary have to tell me the fee in advance?
faqs.a: You should always ask for the total in writing before the appointment, itemized between the notarial act fee and any travel or service charges.

posts.title: Remote Online Notarization (RON) in Florida
posts.metaTitle: Remote Online Notarization in Florida: How RON Works & How to Register (2026)
posts.metaDesc: How remote online notarization works in Florida, what it costs, the $25,000 RON bond and E&O requirement, and how a notary registers under Fla. Stat. 117.225.
keywords: how to become a remote online notary in florida
posts.excerpt: Florida was among the first states to authorize RON. Here is how a session actually works, and what a notary must do to offer it.

sections.html:
Remote Online Notarization lets a notary and a signer complete a notarization over live audio-video from different locations. It is authorised in Florida under Chapter 117, Part II. The signer's identity is confirmed through credential analysis and knowledge-based authentication, the entire session is recorded, and the recording is retained.

RON is not the same as emailing a scanned document to a notary. It is a live, recorded, identity-verified session on an approved platform.

Three formats get conflated constantly:

  • Traditional — paper document, wet ink signature, physical seal, everyone in the same room.
  • IPEN (in-person electronic notarization) — everyone is still in the same room, but the document and signatures are electronic. Authorised by §117.021, and it requires no separate registration beyond your standard commission. §117.021(4) gives the notary the right to select the technology.
  • RON — the signer is remote, appearing by audio-video. This requires separate registration with the Department of State.

The difference that matters: remote means registration; electronic-but-in-person does not.

sections.h: What a notary needs to offer RON
sections.html:
Under §117.225, a Florida notary registering as an online notary public must:

  • Hold a current traditional notary commission
  • Complete a state-approved RON education course
  • Obtain a separate $25,000 surety bond — this is in addition to the $7,500 traditional bond
  • Carry errors & omissions insurance of at least $25,000
  • Register with the Department of State and pay the filing fee
  • Use a Department-registered RON technology provider

The trap: your RON registration expires on the same day as your underlying notary commission, regardless of when you registered it. There is no grace period. If your commission lapses, you reapply as a notary and then reapply for RON from scratch.

A Florida notary may charge up to $25 per online notarial act under §117.275 — higher than the $10 traditional cap, reflecting the platform and retention costs. Travel is irrelevant for RON, but platform fees, document handling, and signing-agent services remain separate and uncapped.

Not everything can be done remotely. Certain documents and county recording practices still require wet signatures, and in real estate the lender and title underwriter decide the format per file — not the notary and not the signer.

faqs.q: Is remote online notarization legal in Florida?
faqs.a: Yes. Florida authorises remote online notarization under Chapter 117, Part II of the Florida Statutes. The notary must be separately registered as an online notary public with the Florida Department of State.

faqs.q: How much does a remote online notarization cost in Florida?
faqs.a: Florida caps the online notarial act at $25 under Fla. Stat. 117.275, compared to $10 for a traditional act. Platform fees and any signing-agent services are separate and not capped.

faqs.q: What does a Florida notary need to perform remote online notarizations?
faqs.a: A current traditional commission, a state-approved RON education course, a separate $25,000 surety bond, at least $25,000 in errors and omissions insurance, registration with the Department of State, and use of a registered RON technology provider.

faqs.q: Does a Florida RON registration expire with the notary commission?
faqs.a: Yes. The online notary registration expires on the same day as the underlying notary commission regardless of when it was filed, and there is no grace period. If the commission lapses, both must be applied for again.

faqs.q: What is the difference between RON and IPEN?
faqs.a: RON means the signer appears remotely by audio-video and requires separate state registration. IPEN, in-person electronic notarization, means everyone is physically present but the document and signature are electronic. IPEN is authorised under Fla. Stat. 117.021 and requires no separate registration.

posts.title: How to Become a Loan Signing Agent in Florida
posts.metaTitle: How to Become a Loan Signing Agent in Florida (2026): Steps, Cost & Earnings
posts.metaDesc: What a notary signing agent actually does, the background screening and E&O that platforms require, realistic per-signing fees in Florida, and how to get assigned work.
keywords: how to become a loan signing agent in florida
how much do loan signing agents make
posts.excerpt: A loan signing agent is a notary who handles mortgage closing packages. The commission is the easy part; the credentials are what gate the work.

sections.html:
A notary signing agent presents a mortgage closing package to a borrower, directs them where to sign and date, performs the notarizations, and returns the executed package to the title company or lender. A typical refinance package runs 100–200 pages and takes 45–90 minutes at the table.

What the job is not: giving advice. A signing agent may identify a document by name and point to where it is signed. Explaining what a term means for the borrower's situation, or advising whether they should sign, is the unauthorised practice of law.

sections.h: What you need beyond the commission
sections.html:
The Florida commission is the entry ticket. The work is gated by what the platforms and title companies require on top:

  • A current background screening. Most platforms require one completed within the last 12 months. This is the single most common reason applications sit unprocessed.
  • Errors & omissions insurance. Not required by Florida law, but effectively mandatory. Coverage of $25,000 is a common floor; $100,000 clears essentially every published threshold, and some platforms require it for real estate work specifically.
  • A signing agent certification. Not a legal requirement. Many title companies filter for it.
  • A dual-tray laser printer. Loan packages print on both letter and legal paper. This is not optional equipment.
  • A scanner for same-day scanbacks.

Realistic per-signing fees, depending on product and market:

  • Refinance — $85–$150
  • Purchase, buyer package — $100–$200
  • Seller-only — $75–$125
  • Reverse mortgage — $125–$275 (highest liability; never accept refinance pricing)
  • Loan modification — $50–$125

Subtract printing, toner, paper, mileage, and shipping. Net is meaningfully lower than gross, and volume depends entirely on interest rates.

Assignments come from signing services and title companies, not from consumer directories. A directory listing produces general notary work — a $10 acknowledgment plus a travel fee — not loan closings.

Loan signing work is dispatched. You register with signing service platforms, they send you assignments, and they keep a spread. Separately, independent title companies and closing law firms maintain their own lists of notaries they call directly, which is where the better fees are.

If you are a Florida notary looking for signing assignments, RON Closing dispatches both remote online sessions and in-person signings to commissioned Florida notaries.

faqs.q: How much do loan signing agents make in Florida?
faqs.a: Per-signing fees typically range from $85 to $150 for a refinance, $100 to $200 for a purchase package, and $125 to $275 for a reverse mortgage. Printing, toner, mileage, and shipping come out of that, and volume depends heavily on interest rates.

faqs.q: Do you need a certification to be a loan signing agent in Florida?
faqs.a: No. Florida law requires only a notary commission. However, most signing services and title companies require a background screening completed within the last 12 months, errors and omissions insurance, and often a signing agent certification before assigning work.

faqs.q: How much E&O insurance does a loan signing agent need?
faqs.a: Florida does not require any. In practice, $25,000 is a common minimum among signing platforms, and $100,000 clears essentially every published threshold. Some platforms require $100,000 specifically for real estate signings.

faqs.q: Can a notary signing agent explain loan documents to a borrower?
faqs.a: No. A signing agent may identify a document by name and indicate where to sign. Explaining what a document means for the borrower's situation, or advising whether to sign, is the unauthorised practice of law.

faqs.q: Do I need a special printer to be a loan signing agent?
faqs.a: Yes, practically speaking. Loan packages print on both letter and legal size paper, so a dual-tray laser printer is standard equipment, along with a scanner for same-day scanbacks.

posts.title: Florida Deed Witness Requirements
posts.metaTitle: Do Florida Deeds Need Witnesses? Two-Witness Rule Explained (Fla. Stat. 689.01)
posts.metaDesc: Florida deeds require two subscribing witnesses under Fla. Stat. 689.01. Mortgages do not. Here is the difference, and when a notary may serve as one of the witnesses.
keywords: do deeds need witnesses in florida
can a notary be a witness in florida
posts.excerpt: Deeds need two witnesses. Mortgages do not. Getting this wrong is the most common Florida closing error there is.

sections.html:
Fla. Stat. §689.01 requires that a conveyance of an interest in Florida real property be signed in the presence of two subscribing witnesses. A deed executed without them is defective and can create serious title problems.

This applies to deeds — warranty deeds, quit claim deeds, and similar instruments conveying an interest in land.

A mortgage does not carry the same statutory witness requirement. Under §697.02, a Florida mortgage is a lien on property, not a conveyance of a freehold estate, and §695.26(1)(f) expressly exempts mortgages from the witness-signature requirement for recording. Fannie Mae's Florida security instrument now treats the witness lines as optional for exactly this reason.

But follow the closing instructions, not the statute. Virtually every Florida lender still prints two witness lines on the mortgage, and the title company's instructions require them completed. An unusable loan file is an unusable loan file regardless of what the statute permits.

sections.h: Can the notary be a witness?
sections.html:
In Florida, yes — but only if the notary actually observed the signer sign. The notary signs twice: once on a witness line, once in the notarial certificate.

The condition matters. A notary who merely takes an acknowledgment — where the signer confirms a signature they made earlier, outside the notary's presence — did not witness the signing and cannot serve as a subscribing witness to it.

You still need a second, independent witness either way. A witness should not be a party to the transaction or have a financial interest in it.

Witnesses may also appear remotely by audio-video under §689.01(2)–(3).

Confirm the witness requirement in writing with the title company before any purchase or seller signing. Ask specifically: how many witnesses, and may the notary serve as one. Ten seconds of email saves a re-draw.

Note that leases no longer require witnesses following the 2020 amendment to §689.01.

faqs.q: Do deeds need to be witnessed in Florida?
faqs.a: Yes. Fla. Stat. 689.01 requires a conveyance of an interest in Florida real property to be signed in the presence of two subscribing witnesses. A deed executed without them is defective.

faqs.q: Do Florida mortgages require witnesses?
faqs.a: Not statutorily. A mortgage is a lien rather than a conveyance under Fla. Stat. 697.02, and Fla. Stat. 695.26(1)(f) exempts mortgages from the witness requirement for recording. However, most lenders still print witness lines and closing instructions typically require them completed.

faqs.q: Can a notary be a witness in Florida?
faqs.a: Yes, if the notary actually observed the signer sign the document. The notary signs twice, once as a witness and once in the notarial certificate. A notary who only takes an acknowledgment of a signature made earlier did not witness the signing and cannot serve as a subscribing witness.

faqs.q: How many witnesses does a Florida deed need?
faqs.a: Two subscribing witnesses. If the notary personally observed the signing and serves as one, a second independent witness is still required.

faqs.q: Do leases need witnesses in Florida?
faqs.a: No. Florida amended Fla. Stat. 689.01 in 2020 to remove the two-witness requirement for leases.

posts.title: How to Renew a Florida Notary Commission
posts.metaTitle: How to Renew a Florida Notary Commission (2026): Timeline, Cost & What Lapses
posts.metaDesc: When to start renewing a Florida notary commission, what it costs, what happens if it lapses, and why a lapse also terminates your Remote Online Notary registration.
posts.excerpt: A Florida commission runs four years and does not renew itself. Letting it lapse costs more than renewing on time.

sections.html:
A Florida notary commission runs four years from the date of issue. Renewal is not automatic and the state does not guarantee a reminder.

Begin roughly 90 days before expiration. That leaves room for the bond, any required education, processing, and delivery of a new seal without a gap in your authority to notarize.

You can confirm your own expiration date in this register or through the Department of State.

Renewal broadly mirrors the original application: a new $7,500 surety bond for the new four-year term under §117.01(6), a renewal application filed with the Department of State, the filing fee, and a new seal reflecting the new commission number and expiration date.

Education obligations differ between first-time applicants and renewing notaries. Confirm your current requirement rather than assuming it carries over.

sections.h: What happens if you let it lapse
sections.html:
There is no grace period. Once the commission expires you are not a notary, and any notarization performed after that date is invalid.

A lapse means reapplying as a new notary rather than renewing — which may pull in first-time education requirements.

The expensive part: a lapsed commission also terminates your Remote Online Notary registration. RON registration expires on the same day as the underlying commission regardless of when it was filed. Restoring RON means redoing the course, the separate $25,000 RON bond, the $25,000 E&O, and the registration from scratch.

sections.h: Renew the commission early if you hold RON
sections.html:
Because RON registration inherits the commission's expiration date, registering for RON late in a commission term buys you only the remainder of that term.

If you plan to offer remote online notarization, it is usually worth renewing the underlying commission first, so the RON registration rides a fresh four-year term instead of expiring in a few months.

faqs.q: How do I renew my Florida notary commission?
faqs.a: File a renewal application with the Florida Department of State, obtain a new $7,500 surety bond for the new four-year term, pay the filing fee, and get a new seal showing the new commission number and expiration date. Start about 90 days before expiration.

faqs.q: What happens if my Florida notary commission expires?
faqs.a: There is no grace period. You are no longer a notary and any notarization performed after expiration is invalid. You must reapply as a new notary rather than renew, which may trigger first-time education requirements.

faqs.q: Does my RON registration expire when my notary commission expires?
faqs.a: Yes. A Florida Remote Online Notary registration expires on the same day as the underlying notary commission, regardless of when the RON registration was filed. There is no grace period, and restoring it requires redoing the course, the $25,000 RON bond, the E&O coverage, and the registration.

faqs.q: How long is a Florida notary commission valid?
faqs.a: Four years from the date of issue.

faqs.q: Should I renew my commission early if I want to offer RON?
faqs.a: Often yes. Because RON registration inherits the commission's expiration date, registering late in a term gives you only the remaining months. Renewing the commission first lets the RON registration ride a fresh four-year term.

posts.title: What Is a Mobile Notary?
posts.metaTitle: What Is a Mobile Notary? What They Do, What They Cost & When to Use One
posts.metaDesc: A mobile notary travels to you. Here is what they can and cannot do, what they charge in Florida, and when a mobile notary is the right choice over a bank or shipping store.
posts.excerpt: A mobile notary is a commissioned notary who comes to you. The notarial act is the same; you are paying for the travel.

sections.html:
A mobile notary is a commissioned notary public who travels to the signer — a home, hospital, care facility, office, jail, or coffee shop — rather than requiring the signer to come to them.

The notarial act is identical to one performed at a bank. The notary verifies identity, witnesses the signature or takes the acknowledgment, completes the certificate, and applies the seal. What differs is convenience.

• Hospital and care facility signings — powers of attorney, advance directives, healthcare surrogate designations for someone who cannot travel
  • Real estate closings outside a title office, or after hours
  • Estate documents — wills, trusts, deeds where multiple signers and witnesses must be assembled
  • Time-sensitive documents after banks have closed
  • Multiple signers in one place, where bringing everyone to a branch is impractical

Florida caps the notarial act at $10 (§117.05). Travel is not capped. A typical mobile notary quote in Florida runs $40–$100 depending on distance, time of day, and number of documents — $10 of which is the act, the rest travel and convenience.

That is entirely lawful, provided the fee is disclosed to you beforehand. Ask for the total in writing, itemized. See what a Florida notary can charge.

sections.h: What a mobile notary cannot do
sections.html:
This matters more than most people realise. A Florida notary may not:

  • Give legal advice or explain what a document means for your situation
  • Choose or prepare a document for you
  • Notarize a signature when the signer is not present
  • Notarize their own signature, or a document in which they have a financial interest
  • Certify a copy of a vital record such as a birth or death certificate

If a notary is advising you on what to sign, that is the practice of law, and they should not be doing it.

You can search this register by county, city, or ZIP code for commissioned Florida notaries. Every entry shows the commission number and expiration date so you can verify it independently with the Department of State before your appointment.

faqs.q: What is a mobile notary?
faqs.a: A mobile notary is a commissioned notary public who travels to the signer's location rather than requiring the signer to come to an office. The notarial act itself is identical to one performed at a bank.

faqs.q: How much does a mobile notary cost in Florida?
faqs.a: Typically $40 to $100. Florida caps the notarial act at $10, but travel and convenience fees are not capped and make up the rest. The fee should be disclosed in advance.

faqs.q: Can a mobile notary come to a hospital?
faqs.a: Yes. Hospital and care facility signings are among the most common uses for a mobile notary, particularly for powers of attorney, advance directives, and healthcare surrogate designations.

faqs.q: Can a notary tell me what my document means?
faqs.a: No. Explaining a document's legal effect or advising whether to sign is the practice of law. A Florida notary may identify a document by name and indicate where to sign, and nothing more.

faqs.q: Can a notary certify a copy of a birth certificate in Florida?
faqs.a: No. A Florida notary may not certify copies of vital records such as birth or death certificates. Certified copies must be obtained from the issuing agency.

posts.title: Notary Directories and Signing Platforms Compared
posts.metaTitle: Best Notary Directories & Signing Service Platforms (2026 Comparison)
posts.metaDesc: A plain comparison of notary directories and signing service platforms: what each type actually does, what they cost notaries, and which produce paid loan signing work.
posts.excerpt: Directories and signing services are different businesses. Confusing them is why notaries pay for listings that never produce work.

sections.html:
Notaries routinely pay for the wrong product because these are used interchangeably. They are not the same.

A directory is consumer-facing. Members of the public search it and contact the notary directly. It produces general notary work — a $10 acknowledgment plus a travel fee. Notaries pay to be listed or to be placed higher.

A signing service is business-facing and largely invisible to the public. Title companies and lenders place orders; the platform dispatches them to notaries and keeps a spread. It produces loan signings at $85–$200. Registration is generally free; the platform is paid from the spread.

The practical consequence: a directory listing will not get you loan signing work. If your goal is closings, register with signing services. If your goal is local walk-in work, a directory helps.

Published rates across the established notary directories generally fall between roughly $79 and $500 per year, depending on placement and market. Common structures include a flat annual membership, tiered placement positions, per-county add-ons, and premium top-of-page slots priced by how competitive the market is.

Worth knowing before you buy: several long-standing directories are widely reported by working notaries to produce little assignment volume. Ask for traffic or lead figures before paying for placement, and be sceptical of any directory that will not provide them.

• Does listing cost anything? A directory that charges for basic inclusion has a smaller database, which means less traffic, which means fewer leads.
  • Is the data verified? Listings built from state commission records can be checked against the issuing authority. Self-reported listings cannot.
  • Can you see the fee structure before signing up?
  • Does it produce actual work, or only visibility? These are different promises.
  • Can you remove yourself easily?

State Notary Agent is a free public directory of commissioned Florida notaries, built from Florida Department of State commission records. Basic inclusion costs nothing and searching costs nothing. Notaries may claim an entry at no charge to add services and contact details, and optional paid placement is published openly on the rate card.

It is not a signing service and does not dispatch loan closings. Florida notaries seeking signing assignments — remote online sessions or in-person appointments — should look to RON Closing, which dispatches both to commissioned Florida notaries.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a notary directory and a signing service?
faqs.a: A directory is consumer-facing: the public searches it and contacts the notary directly, producing general notary work. A signing service is business-facing: title companies place orders and the platform dispatches them to notaries, producing loan signings at $85 to $200. Directory listings do not generally produce loan signing work.

faqs.q: Do notary directories actually get you work?
faqs.a: Directories produce general notary work such as acknowledgments and mobile appointments. They rarely produce loan signing assignments, which are dispatched through signing services. Several long-standing paid directories are reported by working notaries to produce little volume, so ask for traffic figures before paying.

faqs.q: How much do notary directories cost?
faqs.a: Published rates generally run between about $79 and $500 per year depending on placement and market competitiveness, using structures such as flat annual membership, tiered placement, per-county add-ons, and premium top-of-page slots.

faqs.q: Is State Notary Agent free?
faqs.a: Yes. Searching the register is free, basic inclusion is free because it is built from Florida Department of State public commission records, and claiming an entry costs nothing. Optional paid placement is published openly on the rate card.

faqs.q: Where do Florida notaries find loan signing work?
faqs.a: Through signing service platforms that dispatch assignments from title companies and lenders, and by building direct relationships with independent title companies and closing law firms. Florida notaries can also receive remote online and in-person signing assignments through RON Closing.
